blocks.content: 1. The Problem: Naive Modulo Hashing Breaks on Every Scaling Event
blocks.text: 1. The Problem: Naive Modulo Hashing Breaks on Every Scaling Event

blocks.content: When you have multiple servers and need to decide which one handles which request, how do you do it without reshuffling everything every time a server is added or removed? Consistent hashing exists specifically to solve this problem.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025894-257844640.png
blocks.alt: Adding just one server to a modulo-hashed pool changes the divisor for every single key at once

blocks.content: The obvious approach is simple modulo hashing: with N servers, a key's server is hash(key) % N. With 4 servers and a key that hashes to 17, 17 % 4 = 1, so it goes to server 1, clean and simple. The problem appears the moment N changes. Scale from 4 servers to 5, and the formula becomes hash(key) % 5. The key's hash value never changed, but because the divisor did, almost every single key now maps to a different server than before.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025895-84783701.png
blocks.alt: A 75% reshuffle of keys turns a routine scaling event into a self-inflicted database overload

blocks.content: Picture this in a cache system holding millions of cached objects. After adding one new server, most requests now get routed to servers that were never asked to cache that data before. Those servers have nothing cached yet, so nearly every one of those requests becomes a cache miss, all landing on the database at once, a phenomenon commonly called a cache miss storm, triggered purely by adding capacity, the opposite of what that operation was supposed to achieve.
2. The Hash Ring: Consistent Hashing's Core Idea
blocks.text: 2. The Hash Ring: Consistent Hashing's Core Idea

blocks.content: Consistent hashing solves the remapping problem directly: when a server is added or removed, only the keys on the immediately neighboring segment move, everything else stays exactly where it was.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396026160-952280391.png
blocks.alt: A new post office only ever takes over the one arc immediately next to it, every other office keeps its existing territory untouched

blocks.content: Imagine post offices placed around a circular city. Each post office handles every address in the arc from itself to the next office, going clockwise. If a new post office opens between two existing ones, it takes over only the addresses in that one arc, every other post office is completely unaffected. That circular city is the hash ring.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396026164-925157827.png
blocks.alt: Bending the hash space into a circle is the one structural change that makes minimal remapping possible

blocks.content: To build this structure concretely: take the complete range of a hash function's output, for example SHA-1's 0 to 2^160 minus 1, called the hash space, and instead of treating it as a straight line, connect the beginning and the end together to form a circle. This circular structure is the hash ring.
3. Placing Servers and Keys on the Ring
blocks.text: 3. Placing Servers and Keys on the Ring

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272578593-23612179.png
blocks.alt: Servers and keys share the exact same ring and the exact same hash function

blocks.content: Using the same hash function, servers are placed on the ring based on their IP address or name, and keys are placed on the same ring based on their own hash value. Unlike the modulo approach, no modulo operation is used at all here, a server or key's position on the ring is simply wherever its raw hash value lands.
4. Server Lookup: Walking Clockwise
blocks.text: 4. Server Lookup: Walking Clockwise

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396026908-141755535.png
blocks.alt: A single, consistent rule finds the right server for any key: walk clockwise until you hit one

blocks.content: To find the server responsible for any key, start at that key's position on the ring and move clockwise until the first server is encountered, that server stores the key. This is the entire rule, and it applies identically no matter how many servers exist or where they happen to sit on the ring.
5. Adding a Server, Step by Step
blocks.text: 5. Adding a Server, Step by Step

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396026909-609562095.png
blocks.alt: A new server only ever claims the keys sitting in the one gap it was inserted into

blocks.content: This is where consistent hashing earns its name: when a new server is added to the ring, only the keys that fall between the new server and its clockwise predecessor need to move to it. Every other key still encounters the exact same server it always did while walking clockwise, and stays completely untouched.

["Step 1: hash the new server's name or IP, and place it on the ring at that position, exactly like any other server","Step 2: walk counter-clockwise from the new server's position until you reach the previous existing server, everything in that arc is the affected range","Step 3: for every key whose position falls inside that specific arc, reassign it to the new server; keys were previously reaching the old predecessor by walking clockwise, they now reach the new server first instead","Step 4: every key outside that arc still hits the same server first while walking clockwise, so it requires zero changes at all"]
items: Step 1: hash the new server's name or IP, and place it on the ring at that position, exactly like any other server
Step 2: walk counter-clockwise from the new server's position until you reach the previous existing server, everything in that arc is the affected range

Step 3: for every key whose position falls inside that specific arc, reassign it to the new server; keys were previously reaching the old predecessor by walking clockwise, they now reach the new server first instead
Step 4: every key outside that arc still hits the same server first while walking clockwise, so it requires zero changes at all

blocks.content: Concretely: with server0, server1, server2, server3 already on the ring and key0 sitting in the arc just before server0, adding server4 into that same arc, between server3 and server0, means key0 now reaches server4 first while walking clockwise instead of server0. Key1, key2, and key3, sitting in completely different arcs, still reach whichever server they always did, and never move.
6. Removing a Server, Step by Step
blocks.text: 6. Removing a Server, Step by Step

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396026163-331731331.png
blocks.alt: Removing a server only affects the keys that were assigned specifically to it

blocks.content: Removal works the same way in reverse: when a server is removed, only the keys that were assigned to it need to be reassigned, they move clockwise to whichever server comes next on the ring. Every key that was never assigned to the removed server keeps mapping to exactly the same server as before.

["Step 1: locate the server being removed on the ring, and note the arc it currently owns, from its counter-clockwise predecessor up to its own position","Step 2: remove that server from the ring entirely","Step 3: every key that was inside the removed server's arc now walks clockwise and lands on whatever server comes next, since the removed server is no longer there to stop at","Step 4: every key that belonged to a different server's arc is entirely unaffected, that arc and its owning server never changed"]
items: Step 1: locate the server being removed on the ring, and note the arc it currently owns, from its counter-clockwise predecessor up to its own position
Step 2: remove that server from the ring entirely
Step 3: every key that was inside the removed server's arc now walks clockwise and lands on whatever server comes next, since the removed server is no longer there to stop at
Step 4: every key that belonged to a different server's arc is entirely unaffected, that arc and its owning server never changed

blocks.content: Concretely: if server1 is removed and key1 was sitting in server1's arc, key1 now walks clockwise past where server1 used to be and lands on server2 instead. Key0, key2, and key3, belonging to other servers' arcs, are completely unaffected and still map to exactly the same servers as before removal.
7. Two Problems With the Basic Approach
blocks.text: 7. Two Problems With the Basic Approach

blocks.content: The basic ring dramatically reduces remapping compared to modulo hashing, but placing each server just once introduces two distinct new problems.
Issue 1: Uneven Partition Sizes
blocks.text: Issue 1: Uneven Partition Sizes

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025896-173964658.png
blocks.alt: Removing one server can hand its entire territory to a single neighbor, doubling that neighbor's load

blocks.content: A partition is the arc of the ring between two neighboring servers. When a server is removed, its neighbor inherits the entire freed arc. If that neighbor's own partition was already a typical size, its partition can now be roughly twice as large as everyone else's, meaning it stores more keys and handles more requests than the rest of the ring, purely as a side effect of one removal.
Issue 2: Uneven Key Distribution
blocks.text: Issue 2: Uneven Key Distribution

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396026159-940057434.png
blocks.alt: Server positions land wherever their hash happens to fall, and that can easily cluster unevenly by pure chance

blocks.content: A second, independent problem: where servers land on the ring is purely a function of their hash value, there is no guarantee those positions spread evenly around the circle. If several servers' hash values happen to cluster close together, one remaining server can end up owning the majority of the ring's arc, receiving most of the keys, while the clustered servers each get very little.
8. Virtual Nodes: The Fix for Both Problems
blocks.text: 8. Virtual Nodes: The Fix for Both Problems

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396026910-926500164.png
blocks.alt: Placing each server at many points instead of one turns one large, luck-dependent partition into many small, evenly-spread ones

blocks.content: Both the uneven-partition and uneven-distribution problems are solved the same way: virtual nodes, also called replicas. Instead of placing a server on the ring once, it is placed many times, at many different hash positions, each one called a virtual node for that physical server. In real systems, each physical server commonly gets hundreds or even thousands of virtual nodes.

Because a server's virtual nodes are spread across many different, effectively random positions on the ring, that server ends up owning many small partitions instead of one single large one, and the overall unevenness from any one partition being unlucky averages out across all of that server's virtual nodes. Server lookup works identically, walk clockwise from the key's position until the first virtual node is found, then use the physical server that virtual node represents.
9. How Many Virtual Nodes Is Enough?
blocks.text: 9. How Many Virtual Nodes Is Enough?

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272590407-214307966.png
blocks.alt: Balance improves quickly at first, then levels off, while memory and metadata cost keeps climbing

blocks.content: As virtual node count increases, key distribution becomes more balanced, measured concretely using standard deviation, how much each server's actual share of keys varies from the average share. A smaller standard deviation means more even load.

{"headers":["Virtual Nodes Per Server","Typical Effect"],"rows":[["1 (the basic approach)","High standard deviation, load can differ by several times between servers purely by chance"],["100 to 200","Standard deviation drops substantially, a well-balanced distribution in practice"],["Well beyond 200","Balance keeps improving only marginally, while memory and metadata overhead keeps growing"]]}

blocks.title: A Real Cost, Not a Free Lunch
blocks.content: Every additional virtual node is another entry the system has to store and look up, more memory and more metadata to maintain. The right number is chosen to balance genuinely improved load distribution against that real, ongoing overhead, not simply maximized.
10. Finding Exactly Which Keys Move
blocks.text: 10. Finding Exactly Which Keys Move

blocks.content: When a new server is added, the specific affected range is found by moving counter-clockwise from the new server's position until the previous server is reached, every key in that specific arc now belongs to the new server, and every other key is untouched. When a server is removed, the same counter-clockwise walk from its position finds the arc that was exclusively its own, those keys move to the next server clockwise, and nothing else changes.
11. Replication Factor: Surviving a Server Failure
blocks.text: 11. Replication Factor: Surviving a Server Failure

blocks.content: So far, each key lives on exactly one server, the first one found walking clockwise. That works fine until that single server crashes, at which point the key is genuinely gone. The replication factor, R, fixes this by storing each key on the next R distinct physical servers found while walking clockwise from the key's position, not just the first one.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396026160-211877838.png
blocks.alt: Collecting the next R distinct servers clockwise from a key's position, instead of stopping at the first one, is what actually survives a node failure

blocks.content: With servers S0, S1, S2, S3 placed clockwise and R = 3, a key hashing to a point just before S1 collects S1, S2, and S3 walking clockwise. That key is now stored on all three; if S1 later fails, S2 and S3 still hold the data, and reads keep working without interruption.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272593665-544957151.png
blocks.alt: Virtual nodes and replication factor answer two genuinely different questions and are tuned independently

blocks.content: Virtual nodes and replication factor solve different problems entirely: virtual nodes decide how evenly keys spread across the available servers, replication factor decides how many servers keep a copy of each key so data survives a server failure. A system tunes both independently, for example 150 virtual nodes per server for balance, alongside R = 3 for durability.
12. Real-World Usage
blocks.text: 12. Real-World Usage

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272595387-436506474.png
blocks.alt: Consistent hashing is running underneath several systems developers interact with constantly

blocks.content: Consistent hashing is everywhere in production distributed systems, and interacting with a distributed cache or database almost always means interacting with it indirectly. Amazon DynamoDB uses it, described in the original Dynamo paper, to distribute data across storage nodes while minimizing rebalancing during scaling events. Apache Cassandra uses the same ring concept for its own partitioning. Memcached client libraries commonly implement consistent hashing purely client-side, so that adding or removing a cache server from the client's configuration doesn't invalidate the entire cache. CDNs use a similar ring-based approach to consistently route a given piece of content to the same edge server.
13. Weighted Consistent Hashing: Servers With Different Capacity
blocks.text: 13. Weighted Consistent Hashing: Servers With Different Capacity

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025897-85670611.png
blocks.alt: Giving a bigger server more virtual nodes lets it own a proportionally larger, fairer share of the ring

blocks.content: Real clusters are frequently heterogeneous, some servers have double the RAM or CPU of others, added at a different time or on a different hardware generation. Giving every server the same number of virtual nodes would send every server the same share of keys regardless of how much traffic it can actually handle, wasting the bigger server's extra capacity.

The fix is simple and directly reuses the mechanism from section 8: give a server virtual nodes proportional to its capacity. A server with twice the capacity of a baseline server gets twice as many virtual nodes, so it naturally ends up owning roughly twice the share of the ring, and therefore roughly twice the share of keys and requests, matching what it can actually serve.
14. An Alternative Approach: Rendezvous Hashing
blocks.text: 14. An Alternative Approach: Rendezvous Hashing

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396026909-393201138.png
blocks.alt: Rendezvous hashing reaches the same goal, minimal remapping, through a scoring rule instead of a ring

blocks.content: Consistent hashing is not the only technique that minimizes remapping. Rendezvous hashing, also called highest random weight hashing, achieves the same goal differently: for a given key, it computes a weight score, typically a hash of the key combined with each server's identity, for every server, and assigns the key to whichever server produces the highest score. No ring, no clockwise walk, no virtual nodes at all.

Adding or removing a server changes the score computation only for that specific server, every other server's score for a given key is completely unaffected, so keys only move away from a removed server or toward a newly added one, exactly the same minimal-remapping property consistent hashing provides, just reached through a different mechanism. Rendezvous hashing trades the ring's fast clockwise lookup for a full O(N) scan across all servers per key, a reasonable tradeoff when the server count is small, but part of why the ring-based approach in this topic remains the more common choice at large scale.

The example below builds exactly the scenario sections 7 through 9 describe: a ring with 3 servers and 3,000 keys, first using just one position per server, then rebuilt using 150 virtual nodes per server, measuring each server's actual share of the keys and the standard deviation across servers both times, to show concretely how dramatically virtual nodes fix the uneven-distribution problem.
Worked Example 1: Scaling a Session Cache Mid-Spike
blocks.text: Worked Example 1: Scaling a Session Cache Mid-Spike

blocks.content: A distributed cache holding session data for a web application runs 4 cache nodes. Under naive modulo hashing, adding a 5th node during a traffic spike would remap roughly 80% of session keys to different nodes, causing nearly every active user to hit a cold cache simultaneously, precisely the cache miss storm from section 1, at the worst possible moment, mid-spike.

Using consistent hashing with 150 virtual nodes per physical node instead, adding the 5th node redistributes only the fraction of keys that mathematically must move, roughly 20% given 5 nodes, and section 9's balance guarantee means that 20% is spread close to evenly rather than dumped disproportionately on whichever node happens to sit next to the new one. Combined with a replication factor of 2 from section 11, even the brief window while those keys are moving still has a second copy of each session available on another node.
Worked Example 2: A Mixed-Hardware Cluster
blocks.text: Worked Example 2: A Mixed-Hardware Cluster

blocks.content: A company inherits a cache cluster with 2 older servers (8 GB RAM each) and adds 2 new servers (32 GB RAM each) during an upgrade. Giving all 4 servers the same 100 virtual nodes each, as section 8 alone would suggest, sends each server roughly a quarter of the keys, wasting most of the new servers' extra capacity while the older servers run proportionally hotter relative to what they can actually hold in memory.

Applying section 13's weighted approach instead, the older servers get 100 virtual nodes each and the newer servers get 400 each, reflecting their 4x memory advantage. The newer servers now organically receive roughly 4x the share of keys the older ones do, matching real capacity rather than treating every physical server as identical.
Common Mistakes
blocks.text: Common Mistakes

blocks.content: ["Using consistent hashing with only one position per server and being surprised when load is still noticeably uneven across servers","Confusing virtual node count with replication factor, they solve genuinely different problems and are tuned independently","Choosing a virtual node count without ever measuring the actual resulting standard deviation, and either under-provisioning balance or over-spending on unnecessary metadata","Forgetting that consistent hashing minimizes remapping but does not eliminate it entirely, a small, predictable fraction of keys always moves when the server count changes","Giving every server the same number of virtual nodes in a cluster with genuinely different hardware capacity, instead of weighting virtual node count by what each server can actually handle"]
items: Using consistent hashing with only one position per server and being surprised when load is still noticeably uneven across servers
Confusing virtual node count with replication factor, they solve genuinely different problems and are tuned independently
Choosing a virtual node count without ever measuring the actual resulting standard deviation, and either under-provisioning balance or over-spending on unnecessary metadata
Forgetting that consistent hashing minimizes remapping but does not eliminate it entirely, a small, predictable fraction of keys always moves when the server count changes
Giving every server the same number of virtual nodes in a cluster with genuinely different hardware capacity, instead of weighting virtual node count by what each server can actually handle

blocks.content: Practice
blocks.text: Practice

blocks.content: A ring has 4 physical servers, each with 100 virtual nodes, and a 5th server is added with the same 100 virtual nodes. Explain, using section 10's method, roughly what fraction of keys you would expect to move, and why that fraction is far smaller than what plain modulo hashing from section 1 would cause for the same change.

A team sets replication factor R = 1 for cost reasons on a system storing financial transaction records. Using section 11, explain concretely what happens to a record the instant its one assigned server fails, and what specifically increasing R would change about that outcome.

Compare consistent hashing and rendezvous hashing from section 14 for a small cluster of exactly 5 servers. Explain one concrete reason a team might still prefer the ring-based approach even at this small scale, and one reason rendezvous hashing's simplicity might be preferred instead.
Key Takeaways
blocks.text: Key Takeaways

blocks.content: Naive modulo hashing remaps almost every key whenever the server count changes, because the divisor itself changes. Consistent hashing fixes this by placing both servers and keys on a circular hash ring and assigning each key to the first server found walking clockwise, so adding or removing a server only ever affects the keys in the one arc immediately next to it.

The basic single-position-per-server ring introduces uneven partitions and uneven key distribution, both fixed by virtual nodes, placing each server at many positions instead of one, typically 100 to 200 per server in practice. Replication factor is a separate, independently tuned mechanism that keeps each key on multiple servers so data survives a single server's failure, and weighted virtual node counts extend the same mechanism to clusters where servers genuinely have different capacity.

Rendezvous hashing reaches the same minimal-remapping goal through a scoring rule instead of a ring, a reasonable alternative at smaller scale. This closes out the Core System Design Concepts module, together with CAP Theorem, Consistency Models, Reliability, and Single Point of Failure, the next module, Load Balancing, builds directly on the ring mechanics covered here.

The load-balancing-algorithms topic's own consistent-hashing section reuses this exact ring, walking through it once more from the specific angle of choosing between load-balancing algorithms, rather than repeating the full mechanics covered in depth here.
